notes.b: Every cell has to take in what it needs and get rid of what it doesn't, and the cell membrane is the gatekeeper that controls this. Understanding what the membrane lets through, and how, explains the three transport processes in this subsection.
points: Every cell is surrounded by a cell membrane: a phospholipid bilayer (a double layer of fat-based molecules) with proteins scattered through it, known as the fluid mosaic model. The membranes around organelles (the small working parts inside a cell) are built the same way.

Materials constantly cross the membrane: cells take in oxygen (O₂), glucose, water and ions (charged particles), and release carbon dioxide (CO₂) and wastes such as urea. This is the transport and transfer of materials across membranes.

The membrane is selectively permeable: it lets some substances through and not others. Small, non-polar molecules (ones with no electrical charge difference across them) such as oxygen and carbon dioxide pass straight through the bilayer.

Water passes through slowly between the phospholipids and quickly through protein water channels (aquaporins). Ions and large polar molecules such as glucose cross only through specific channel or carrier proteins, and large molecules such as proteins and starch cannot cross at all.

Three terms for barriers are easy to mix up. Fully permeable lets water and all solutes through, e.g. the plant cell wall. Semi-permeable (partially permeable) lets water and small molecules through but not larger ones, by the size of its pores, e.g. Visking (dialysis) tubing.
Selectively permeable describes a living membrane, which controls what crosses using its proteins and, unlike the other two, can move substances actively (using energy).

A solution is a solute (e.g. sugar or salt) dissolved in a solvent (water). A concentrated solution has much solute and so a lower concentration of water; a dilute solution has little solute and so a higher concentration of water.
notes.tip: If asked what selectively permeable or semi-permeable means, say that some substances cross and others don't, and give the reason: pore size for semi-permeable, or the membrane's proteins for selectively permeable.

notes.b: Diffusion is the simplest way for substances to move in and out of cells, and it needs no energy from the cell. It is the baseline against which osmosis and active transport are compared.
points: Diffusion is the net movement of molecules or ions from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration, until they are evenly spread. The difference in concentration between two regions is the concentration gradient, and diffusion is movement down the gradient.
Diffusion is passive: it needs no energy from the cell (no ATP, the cell's energy-carrying molecule), because it results from the random movement of particles, which have kinetic (movement) energy.

Individual particles move in all directions, but more move from the crowded region than into it, which gives the net movement. It happens in gases and liquids, in living and non-living systems, with or without a membrane.

Examples in living things: oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli (the air sacs of the lungs) into the blood while carbon dioxide diffuses the other way. There is more on this in Gas exchange and the breathing mechanism.

Carbon dioxide diffuses into a leaf through the stomata (pores) while oxygen diffuses out, and digested food molecules diffuse from the small intestine into the blood. A non-living example is the scent of perfume spreading through a room.

Facilitated diffusion is passive diffusion of ions and polar molecules, such as glucose, down their concentration gradient through specific channel or carrier proteins. They need the proteins because they cannot cross the bilayer directly; it still needs no ATP, e.g. glucose enters red blood cells this way.

Factors that increase the rate of diffusion are a steeper concentration gradient, higher temperature (particles move faster), a larger surface area, a shorter distance (a thinner barrier) and smaller particles.

Exchange surfaces such as alveoli and villi (finger-like folds of the small intestine wall) have a large surface area, a thin wall and a steep gradient kept up by blood flow, so diffusion is fast. Osmosis depends on the same factors.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to define diffusion and give an example. Say "net movement from higher to lower concentration" and name a specific example, such as oxygen into the blood at the alveoli.

notes.b: Water crosses membranes by its own process, because it is a small molecule that moves in and out of cells all the time. Osmosis is diffusion of water, and it explains why cells swell and shrink.
points: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration (a dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (a more concentrated solution) across a semi-permeable (selectively permeable) membrane.
Osmosis is a special case of diffusion: it is the diffusion of water only, and it happens only across a membrane that lets water through but holds back the solute. It is passive and needs no ATP.

Why water moves: solute molecules attract water molecules around them, so fewer water molecules are free to move in a concentrated solution. More free water molecules cross the membrane from the dilute side than from the concentrated side.

This gives a net flow of water into the concentrated solution, until the concentrations are equal or a pressure, such as that of a cell wall, stops it. Water still crosses in both directions; the flow is only greater one way.

Diagram: a U-tube (or beaker) divided by a semi-permeable membrane, dilute solution one side, concentrated sucrose solution the other; larger arrow of water towards the concentrated side, liquid level rising there. Label: semi-permeable membrane, water molecule, sucrose molecule (too large to cross), net movement of water.
notes.tip: Always write "from higher water concentration to lower water concentration" or "from dilute to concentrated solution". Writing "high to low concentration" unqualified reads as the solute moving the wrong way. Water crosses in both directions; only the net flow is one way.

notes.b: Cells sit in watery surroundings, so osmosis decides whether they gain or lose water. Animal cells and plant cells react differently because plant cells have a cell wall.
points: Three terms describe the solution outside a cell compared with the cell's contents. Hypotonic means more dilute than the cell, so water enters the cell; hypertonic means more concentrated than the cell, so water leaves it; isotonic means the same concentration, so there is no net movement.
Animal cells in a hypotonic solution (e.g. pure water) gain water, swell and may burst, because they have no cell wall to hold them in. Red blood cells bursting is called haemolysis.

In a hypertonic solution animal cells lose water and shrink, and red blood cells become shrivelled and spiky (crenated). This is why body fluids must be kept isotonic with cells (osmoregulation). There is more on this in Water.

Plant cells in a hypotonic solution take water into the vacuole (the large water-filled sac in the cell). The cytoplasm is pushed against the cell wall, which resists further swelling, so the cell becomes turgid (firm) and doesn't burst. The pressure of the contents against the wall is turgor pressure.
Plant cells in a hypertonic solution lose water from the vacuole. The cell becomes flaccid (soft), then the cytoplasm and cell membrane shrink away from the cell wall, which is called plasmolysis.

The gap between wall and membrane fills with the outside solution, because the cell wall is fully permeable. Plasmolysis can be reversed (deplasmolysis) if the cell is put back into water before it is damaged.

Diagram: a plant cell in water (turgid, large vacuole, cytoplasm pressed against wall), in isotonic solution (flaccid) and in concentrated solution (plasmolysed, membrane and cytoplasm pulled from wall). Label: cell wall, cell membrane, vacuole, cytoplasm. Also red blood cells in water (swollen, bursting), isotonic (normal disc) and concentrated solution (crenated).
notes.tip: Say what the outside solution is compared with the cell: never call a cell hypertonic without saying compared with what. Plant cells don't burst in water because of the cell wall, and plasmolysis happens only in plant cells; haemolysis and crenation are for red blood cells.

notes.b: Diffusion and osmosis only move things down a gradient, but cells often need to collect substances that are already scarcer outside than inside. Active transport does this by spending energy.
points: Active transport is the movement of molecules or ions across a membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration, against the concentration gradient, using energy from ATP.

Because it needs ATP, active transport happens only in living cells and depends on respiration (the process that makes ATP). It stops or slows if respiration is stopped, e.g. by lack of oxygen, low temperature or a respiratory poison such as cyanide.
Cells that carry out much active transport have many mitochondria (the organelles that make ATP), e.g. root hair cells, cells lining the kidney tubules and cells of the small intestine.
Root hair cells take up mineral ions, e.g. nitrate, from soil water in which they are more dilute than in the cell. There is more on this in Transport in Plants.
Glucose and amino acids are absorbed from the small intestine into the blood, and reabsorbed from the kidney tubules (the tiny tubes that filter blood) into the blood, by active transport.
notes.tip: Exams ask why active transport needs ATP or stops when respiration stops: the carrier proteins need energy from ATP to change shape and move the substance against its gradient. Active transport does not move water; water always moves by osmosis.

notes.b: Active transport is carried out by carrier proteins in the membrane, which act as pumps. Each pump works in the same four steps.
points: 1. The substance binds to a specific carrier protein (a pump) in the membrane, so each pump moves only the substance it fits.
2. ATP made in respiration releases energy, which changes the shape of the carrier protein.
3. The change in shape moves the substance across the membrane and releases it on the other side.
4. The carrier returns to its original shape, ready to pick up another molecule.

Diagram: a carrier protein in a phospholipid bilayer, a molecule binding on the low-concentration side, ATP → ADP + Pi releasing energy, carrier changing shape, molecule released on the high-concentration side. Label: carrier protein, phospholipid bilayer, ATP, direction of movement against the gradient.
notes.tip: When describing active transport, link the steps in order: binding, ATP energy, shape change, release, return to shape.

notes.b: This carrier pump moves two ions in opposite directions at once. It is found in animal cells and is essential for nerves.
points: The sodium–potassium pump is a carrier protein in the membranes of animal cells, including nerve cells. It uses one ATP to pump three sodium ions (Na⁺) out of the cell and two potassium ions (K⁺) into it, both against their concentration gradients.
It keeps Na⁺ high outside the cell and K⁺ high inside, which nerve cells need in order to carry impulses, and it helps control cell volume.

notes.h: Distinguishing diffusion, osmosis and active transport
notes.b: The three processes are easy to confuse, so exams ask you to compare them. Compare them on the same five points each time: energy, direction, what moves, membrane and proteins, and where they happen.
points: Energy: diffusion and osmosis are passive, so they need no ATP; active transport needs ATP from respiration.

Direction: diffusion and osmosis go down a concentration gradient (high to low concentration of the substance moving; for osmosis, the water concentration), whereas active transport goes against it, from low to high.
What moves: diffusion moves any particle, gases and solutes alike; osmosis moves only water; active transport moves particular solutes, mainly ions and small molecules such as glucose, but not water.

Membrane and proteins: diffusion can happen with or without a membrane and needs no proteins for small non-polar molecules; osmosis needs a semi-permeable membrane; active transport needs specific carrier proteins in a living membrane.
Where: diffusion and osmosis happen in living and non-living systems, e.g. Visking tubing, but active transport happens only in living cells, because it depends on respiration.
notes.tip: For "explain the difference" questions, pair the processes point by point (energy, direction, what moves) rather than describing each separately, and give an example of each.

questions.prompt: Define osmosis and state two ways in which it differs from active transport.
questions.model: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration across a semi-permeable membrane. It differs from active transport in that osmosis is passive and needs no ATP, whereas active transport needs energy from ATP made in respiration. Osmosis moves water down a concentration gradient, whereas active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient, from low to high concentration. Osmosis moves only water, whereas active transport moves particular solutes such as ions and glucose.

questions.prompt: Explain what happens to a red blood cell and to a plant cell when each is placed in (i) distilled water and (ii) a concentrated salt solution.
questions.model: (i) In distilled water, a red blood cell takes in water by osmosis, swells and may burst; the bursting is haemolysis. A plant cell takes in water into its vacuole by osmosis. Its cytoplasm is pushed against the cell wall, which resists further swelling, so the cell becomes turgid and does not burst. (ii) In a concentrated salt solution, a red blood cell loses water by osmosis and shrinks, becoming shrivelled and spiky; this is crenation. A plant cell loses water from its vacuole, becomes flaccid, and its cytoplasm and cell membrane shrink away from the cell wall; this is plasmolysis. The space between the wall and the membrane fills with the outside solution, because the cell wall is fully permeable. The cell wall is what stops the plant cell from bursting in water.

questions.prompt: Describe how active transport moves substances across a cell membrane, with reference to the sodium–potassium pump, and explain why it is affected by a lack of oxygen.
questions.model: Active transport moves a molecule or ion across a membrane against its concentration gradient, from low to high concentration. The substance binds to a specific carrier protein in the membrane. ATP made in respiration releases energy, which changes the shape of the carrier protein, moving the substance across the membrane, where it is released. The carrier then returns to its original shape to pick up another molecule. The sodium–potassium pump is an example in animal cells, including nerve cells: it uses one ATP to pump three Na⁺ out of the cell and two K⁺ into it, both against their concentration gradients, keeping Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside. Active transport needs ATP, which comes from respiration. A lack of oxygen stops aerobic respiration, so less ATP is made, and active transport stops or slows.
